final_answer:
Short answer: under the Guidelines it does not matter much which office indicts, because both offices can reach the whole scheme through relevant conduct; what matters is how many counts of conviction (and so how much statutory-maximum headroom) the office can charge. The office to choose is the one with venue over the larger number of false-claim executions, and in practice the district where the greater share of the fraudulent claims or loss occurred. If the facts are truly even, the answer is a toss-up, and the 'whichever district can charge more counts' principle controls.

Reasoning. (1) Venue: health care fraud under 18 U.S.C. 1347 punishes executing or attempting to execute a scheme to defraud a health care benefit program; each execution is chargeable as a separate count. Under 18 U.S.C. 3237(a), an offense begun, continued or completed in more than one district may be prosecuted in any district where it was begun, continued or completed. So each office has venue for the claims submitted, processed or otherwise executed in its own district, and possibly more if a scheme-wide count has contacts in both. Which claims fall in which district is a fact question I could not resolve from the hypothetical. (2) Guidelines: the offense guideline is USSG 2B1.1. Loss (greater of actual or intended loss, in the text since the Nov. 1, 2024 amendment) drives the offense level, with a further enhancement for health care program fraud over $1 million, and abuse of trust under 3B1.3 for a physician. Under 1B1.3(a)(2), for offenses that group under 3D1.2(d) (fraud does), the court counts all acts that were part of the same course of conduct or common scheme or plan, which is not geographically limited. So the Georgia claims count as relevant conduct in a South Carolina prosecution and vice versa; the advisory range is therefore roughly the same either way, computed on total loss from both states. (3) Statutory cap: relevant conduct raises the Guidelines range but not the statutory maximum for the counts of conviction (10 years per 1347 count absent serious bodily injury or death, which I did not verify from the primary text). Under USSG 5G1.2(d), when the range exceeds the highest statutory maximum on any one count, sentences run consecutively to reach the total punishment. So an office that can charge many counts of conviction in its district can deliver the full range, while an office with only one or two counts is capped. Consequently the office with venue over the most executions (usually the one with the larger volume of claims) should indict; a single-district indictment limited to a few counts would be capped even though the other state's conduct inflates the range. (4) Circuit differences: South Carolina sits in the Fourth Circuit and Georgia in the Eleventh, so appellate review differs. The pre-amendment split over whether 'loss' includes intended loss (United States v. Banks, 3d Cir. 2022, and Kisor/Dupree-based arguments) was resolved by the 2024 amendment putting intended loss in the guideline text, so, given the assumption that both judges follow the Guidelines, it should not change the calculation. (5) Double jeopardy and practical limits: after conviction in one district, a second prosecution in the other for the same executions would be barred, though distinct executions (distinct claims) may be separately charged; the first office's use of the other state's conduct as relevant conduct does not itself bar later charges, but a later sentence would be separate and the court may adjust under 5G1.3 for related conduct. Bottom line: indict in the district with the most counts of fraud claims (and likely greatest loss); if equal, either office, with coordination (or a stipulated transfer under Fed. R. Crim. P. 20) as the realistic alternative. Limitation: I could not access the guideline or statute text directly (government sites were blocked), so statutory-maximum and guideline-subsection details rely on secondary descriptions and my background knowledge.
